title: Three weeks for the wrong room
where: ESM, Kirchberg — Conference room Schuman, seventh floor

lines.text: Rain on the plateau since Monday. Behind Lorenzo de' Medici a tram slides down Avenue John F. Kennedy and disappears past the Philharmonie. He has given you forty minutes and looks like a man who intends to use twenty.
lines.plain: It has rained on the Kirchberg plateau since Monday. Behind Lorenzo de' Medici, a tram passes on Avenue John F. Kennedy. He has given you forty minutes. He looks like he plans to use only twenty.

lines.text: Item three. Outsourcing Plan, draft zero point three.
lines.plain: Item three on the agenda. The Outsourcing Plan, draft version 0.3.
g: Outsourcing Plan
the plan for what a project buys from outside, from whom, and on what terms
ref: The Outsourcing Plan defines the what and how for any outsourced products or services.

lines.text: Before you read it. One sentence, in a document nobody can reopen. The platform is bought. Not built.
lines.plain: Before you read it, I want one sentence in a document that nobody can argue with later. The platform is bought. It is not built here.

lines.text: Page two, first paragraph.
lines.plain: That sentence is on page two, in the first paragraph.

lines.text: Four drafts have said that. On Friday somebody asked my architects to price a build option again.
lines.plain: Four different drafts have said that. On Friday, somebody again asked my architects to give a price for building it ourselves.

lines.text: They are asked because they keep offering.
lines.plain: People ask them because your architects keep offering to build it.

lines.text: They offer because nobody ever closed the question.
lines.plain: They offer because nobody ever closed the question properly.

lines.text: It closed on the twenty-fourth of March. Option C. Lorenzo's board signed it.
lines.plain: The question closed on 24 March. Option C was chosen. Lorenzo's board approved it.

lines.text: Bought from outside: platform licence, implementation, migration of fourteen years of LOS data, two releases. Kept inside: requirements, testing, the two interfaces, and anything that touches the audit trail.
lines.plain: This is what we buy from outside: the platform licence, the implementation work, the migration of fourteen years of LOS data, and two releases. This stays inside the ESM: requirements, testing, the two interfaces, and anything that touches the audit trail.
g: data migration
moving records from an old system into a new one without losing or changing them
ref: Identify the deliverables and activities that need to be outsourced, along with the timeframe within which the outsourcing should take place.

lines.text: The audit trail stays. Good. That is the sentence.
lines.plain: The audit trail stays inside the ESM. Good. That is the sentence I wanted.

lines.text: Then tell me why I am in the room. I do not sit on your Steering Committee.
lines.plain: Then tell me why I am here. I am not a member of your Project Steering Committee.

lines.text: Courtesy, mostly. Your board authorises the award in September, and I would rather you saw the criteria than the invoice.
lines.plain: Politeness, mainly. Your board approves the contract award in September. I prefer you to see the selection criteria now, rather than only the bill later.
g: award
the formal decision that gives a contract to one supplier after a tender

lines.text: It is not a courtesy.
lines.plain: It is not politeness.

lines.text: Henry Gantt turns his screen round. One row of a responsibility table, guide page forty-eight. Accountable, the Appropriate Governance Body. Consulted, the Steering Committee, the Project Owner, the Business Manager. Supporting, the Solution Provider. Responsible, the Project Manager.
lines.plain: Henry Gantt turns his screen so everyone can see it. It shows one row of a responsibility table from page 48 of the guide. Accountable: the Appropriate Governance Body. Consulted: the Steering Committee, the Project Owner and the Business Manager. Supporting: the Solution Provider. Responsible: the Project Manager.
g: Appropriate Governance Body
the senior body that approves projects, releases their money and manages the portfolio
RASCI
a table naming who is Responsible, Accountable, Supporting, Consulted and Informed
ref: Outsourcing Plan A C C C I S R I

lines.text: That is wrong. I approve the Business Case, the Charter, the Handbook, the Work Plan, the acceptance plan, the transition plan, the business implementation plan —
lines.plain: That is wrong. I approve the Business Case, the Project Charter, the Project Handbook, the Work Plan, the Deliverables Acceptance Plan, the Transition Plan and the Business Implementation Plan...
ref: Approves key project artefacts (Business Case, Project Charter, Project Handbook, Work Plan, Deliverables Acceptance Plan, Transition Plan, Business Implementation Plan).

lines.text: Read the list again.
lines.plain: Please read that list again.

lines.text: She reads it again. The Outsourcing Plan is not on it. It has never been on it.
lines.plain: Florence reads the list again. The Outsourcing Plan is not on the list. It was never on the list.

lines.text: When an award goes wrong, nobody asks the project. They ask this floor, in a room with the auditors, how a contractor was chosen.
lines.plain: When a contract award goes wrong, nobody asks the project team about it. They ask us on this floor, in a room with the auditors, how the supplier was chosen.
ref: In terms of projects, this is the body with the authority to approve a project, agree its stated objective and release the funding required to implement it.

lines.text: And I am an S. Supporting. On the one plan that decides who builds my platform.
lines.plain: And I am marked S, for Supporting. On the one plan that decides who builds my platform.

lines.text: You review it. You are then accountable for what the contractor does. Those are two different sentences.
lines.plain: You review the plan. After that you are accountable for how the contractor performs. Those are two different things.
ref: Approves the objectives of any outsourced activities and deliverables and becomes accountable for the contractor's performance.

lines.text: And whatever you write in it, the procurement code wins.
lines.plain: And whatever you write in this plan, the ESM procurement rules are stronger than it.
ref: Note that the present plan should be compliant with the relevant organisational rules and procedures.

lines.text: What is the ceiling?
lines.plain: What is the maximum amount?

lines.text: Eight point four million. All in.
lines.plain: 8.4 million euro. That includes everything.

lines.text: And if the tender comes back at nine?
lines.plain: And if the best offer in the tender is nine million euro?

lines.text: Then it comes back to you.
lines.plain: Then it comes back to your board.

lines.text: Zero point three is finished Thursday. Where does it go?
lines.plain: Version 0.3 will be finished on Thursday. Where do you take it?

choice.prompt: Draft v0.3 is finished on Thursday. Where do you take it for approval?
choice.promptPlain: Draft version 0.3 is ready on Thursday. Who approves it?

options.t: To Lorenzo's Corporate Investment Board. The Appropriate Governance Body is Accountable for this plan; the Steering Committee is consulted on it.
options.tPlain: To Lorenzo's Corporate Investment Board. The Appropriate Governance Body is Accountable for the Outsourcing Plan. The Steering Committee is only consulted.

reply.text: Bring the evaluation criteria with it. I am approving a method, not a supplier — and if you ever want me to approve a supplier, I will want to know what left the portfolio to pay for him.
reply.plain: Bring the evaluation criteria with the plan. I approve a method, not a company. And if you ever want me to approve a company, I will ask what other project lost its money to pay for it.

options.why: The Outsourcing Plan is the one PM² plan whose RASCI row ends in an A at the far left: AGB Accountable, PSC Consulted, PO Consulted, BM Consulted, BIG Informed, SP Supporting, PM Responsible, PCT Informed (p.48). The body that releases funding and owns the portfolio also owns the decision to spend it outside the institution. The Project Manager still writes it and the Solution Provider still reviews it.
options.whyPlain: The Outsourcing Plan is the only PM² plan where the Appropriate Governance Body is Accountable. On page 48 the row reads: AGB Accountable, Steering Committee Consulted, Project Owner Consulted, Business Manager Consulted, business group Informed, Solution Provider Supporting, Project Manager Responsible, Core Team Informed. The body that releases the money also decides to spend it outside the organisation. The Project Manager still writes the plan and the Solution Provider still reviews it.
ref: Outsourcing Plan A C C C I S R I

options.t: To the Project Steering Committee. It approved the Handbook, the Work Plan and the Quality Management Plan, so it approves this one too.
options.tPlain: To the Project Steering Committee. It approved the Handbook, the Work Plan and the Quality Management Plan, so it should approve this plan too.

reply.text: It approves almost everything, which is exactly why people put this one in front of it and nobody notices for two years.
reply.plain: The Steering Committee approves nearly everything. That is exactly why people bring this plan to it as well, and nobody notices the mistake for two years.

options.why: The pattern is real and the exception is real. The Steering Committee is Consulted on the Outsourcing Plan, not Accountable (p.48). It stays involved later — under Manage Outsourcing the PSC ensures the contractor is chosen according to the organisation's processes and the criteria defined for the project (p.85) — but ensuring a selection follows the rules is not approving the plan that sets them.
options.whyPlain: The pattern is real, and so is the exception. On page 48 the Steering Committee is Consulted on the Outsourcing Plan, not Accountable. It still has work to do later: during Manage Outsourcing it makes sure the contractor is chosen by the organisation's rules and the project's criteria (page 85). But checking that a selection follows the rules is not the same as approving the plan that writes them.
ref: Outsourcing Plan A C C C I S R I

options.t: To Florence. She is the Project Owner and she approves the key project artefacts.
options.tPlain: To Florence. She is the Project Owner, and the Project Owner approves the key project documents.

reply.text: I have just read my own list out loud in front of three people. It is not on it. Do not put me somewhere the guide did not.
reply.plain: I just read my list of approvals out loud in front of three people. This plan is not on the list. Do not give me an approval the guide did not give me.

options.why: The Project Owner's list of key artefacts on p.25 is specific and complete: Business Case, Project Charter, Project Handbook, Work Plan, Deliverables Acceptance Plan, Transition Plan, Business Implementation Plan. The Outsourcing Plan is deliberately absent. On p.48 the PO is Consulted, alongside the Business Manager and the Steering Committee.
options.whyPlain: Page 25 lists exactly which key documents the Project Owner approves: Business Case, Project Charter, Project Handbook, Work Plan, Deliverables Acceptance Plan, Transition Plan and Business Implementation Plan. The Outsourcing Plan is missing on purpose. On page 48 the Project Owner is only Consulted, like the Business Manager and the Steering Committee.
ref: Approves key project artefacts (Business Case, Project Charter, Project Handbook, Work Plan, Deliverables Acceptance Plan, Transition Plan, Business Implementation Plan).

options.t: To Leonardo. He becomes accountable for the contractor's performance, so he should approve the plan that picks one.
options.tPlain: To Leonardo. He becomes accountable for how the contractor performs, so he should approve the plan that chooses one.

reply.text: I would take it. That is the problem with giving it to me. My division wants a supplier who agrees with my architects, and somebody outside this project should be allowed to mind about that.
reply.plain: I would sign it. That is exactly the problem. My division wants a supplier who agrees with my architects. Somebody outside the project should be allowed to worry about that.

options.why: Both halves of the confusion are true, which is what makes it tempting. The Solution Provider does become accountable for the contractor's performance and does approve the objectives of outsourced activities (p.26) — but on the plan itself he only Supports, and the Project Manager is Responsible for preparing it (p.48). Separating who selects from who lives with the selection is the control.
options.whyPlain: Both halves of this are true, which is why it is tempting. The Solution Provider does become accountable for the contractor's performance, and does approve the objectives of outsourced work (page 26). But on the plan itself he only Supports. The Project Manager prepares it and the governance body approves it (page 48). Keeping the chooser separate from the person who lives with the choice is the control.
ref: Approves the objectives of any outsourced activities and deliverables and becomes accountable for the contractor's performance.

you.o: Responsible for preparing the Outsourcing Plan. Draft v0.3 is written and, until this afternoon, aimed at the wrong approver.
you.k: Knows the scope, the ceiling and the September award date. Has just learned who signs.
you.w: Wants the plan approved in time for a tender file that closes in July.
you.f: Afraid three weeks of drafting was shaped for a committee that only gets consulted.

leonardo.o: Solution Provider. Supports the Outsourcing Plan and reviews it; accountable later for the contractor's performance.
leonardo.k: Knows the Business Case chose to buy, and that his architects are still asked to price a build.
leonardo.w: Wants one unarguable sentence saying the platform is bought, not built.
leonardo.f: Afraid procurement reinterprets the decision in September and his division ends up building it.

medici.o: AGB chair. Accountable for approving the Outsourcing Plan and for authorising the award.
medici.k: Knows the ceiling is 8.4 million and that no supplier has been chosen yet.
medici.w: Wants to see the evaluation criteria before he sees any invoice.
medici.f: Afraid of sitting with auditors explaining a selection nobody wrote down in advance.

nightingale.o: Project Owner and PSC chair. Consulted on this plan; approves seven other key artefacts.
nightingale.k: Has just discovered the Outsourcing Plan is not on the list she approves.
nightingale.w: Wants a date for approval so the tender is not the thing that slips.
nightingale.f: Afraid another approving body means another month before anything is bought.

gantt.o: Project Support Office. Keeps the responsibility matrix and minutes this meeting.
gantt.k: Knows the p.48 row by heart and knows why it surprises people.
gantt.w: Wants the approval route recorded correctly before anyone drafts further.
gantt.f: Afraid a plan approved by the wrong body has to be approved twice.

note: Guide check: section 6.5, p.48. The Outsourcing Plan defines the what and how for anything the project buys outside, sets the contracting strategies and fixes responsibilities for the whole outsourcing lifecycle, and must comply with the organisation's own procurement rules. It is the anomaly in the PM² responsibility matrix. RASCI: AGB A, PSC C, PO C, BM C, BIG I, SP S, PM R, PCT I. Approver: the Appropriate Governance Body — here Lorenzo de' Medici's Corporate Investment Board — not the Project Steering Committee and not the Project Owner. The Project Manager prepares it; the Solution Provider reviews it. Note that the Project Owner's own list of key artefacts on p.25 pointedly omits it. Manage Outsourcing keeps the same anomaly in the Executing Phase: AGB A, PM R (p.85). Pages 24, 25, 26, 48.
notePlain: Rule: the Outsourcing Plan says what the project buys from outside, how it will be bought, and who is responsible at each step. It must follow the organisation's own purchasing rules (page 48). This is the one plan where the responsibility table is different from all the others. RASCI: Appropriate Governance Body Accountable, Steering Committee Consulted, Project Owner Consulted, Business Manager Consulted, business group Informed, Solution Provider Supporting, Project Manager Responsible, Core Team Informed. Approver: the Appropriate Governance Body, which here is Lorenzo de' Medici's Corporate Investment Board. Not the Steering Committee. Not the Project Owner. The Project Manager writes it and the Solution Provider reviews it. Page 25 lists the key documents the Project Owner approves, and this plan is not in that list. The same unusual pattern returns later in Manage Outsourcing on page 85. Pages 24, 25, 26 and 48.

title: Forty minutes on a stage
where: ESM, Kirchberg — Room Werner, fourth floor

lines.text: Thunder over the plateau at half past nine in the morning, which May does not usually do. The lights in Room Werner come on by themselves.
lines.plain: There is thunder over the Kirchberg plateau at 09:30 in the morning. That is unusual for May. The lights in Room Werner switch themselves on.

lines.text: Eleven vendor presentations in Amsterdam last week. I know what good looks like now. Let me write the technical criteria.
lines.plain: Last week I watched eleven suppliers present in Amsterdam. Now I know what a good product looks like. Let me write the technical criteria.

lines.text: What does good look like?
lines.plain: What does a good product look like?

lines.text: A firm called Levallois Systems. Their engine configured a new instrument on stage in about forty minutes.
lines.plain: A company called Levallois Systems. On stage, their software set up a new lending product in about forty minutes.

lines.text: On stage. With a prepared instrument, a demonstration dataset and no reconciliation.
lines.plain: On stage. With a lending product prepared in advance, demonstration data, and no reconciliation at the end.

lines.text: Say that again. Slowly.
lines.plain: Please say that sentence again, slowly.

lines.text: It can be done, so we are allowed to ask for it. We can ask for what we have watched a supplier do.
lines.plain: It is possible, so we are allowed to require it. We can require what we have seen a supplier do.

lines.text: You have watched one supplier. Write the criteria around what that supplier does and the tender has a winner before it opens. Everybody else pays to lose.
lines.plain: You have seen one supplier. If you write the criteria to describe what that supplier does, the tender already has a winner before it starts. The other companies spend money on an offer that cannot win.
ref: List the evaluation criteria for contractors. This ensures that a contractor is selected on the basis of pre-set criteria and that no single person or group influences the decision.

lines.text: Nobody says the other thing for a while. Nikola Tesla's badge is a contractor's badge. Levallois pays him. He is sitting at the table where the evaluation criteria are being drafted.
lines.plain: For a while nobody says the other problem out loud. Nikola Tesla has a contractor's badge. Levallois Systems pays his salary. He is sitting at the table where the evaluation criteria are being written.
g: conflict of interest
when someone's own interest could affect a decision they help to make

lines.text: Nikola. You will not be on the evaluation panel.
lines.plain: Nikola, you will not be a member of the evaluation panel.

lines.text: I have not asked to be.
lines.plain: I did not ask to be on it.

lines.text: I know. I am putting it in the plan today, while it is still nothing, rather than in September when it would be a favour.
lines.plain: I know. I am writing it into the plan today, while it costs nothing. In September it would look like a favour to someone.

lines.text: Then take my architecture note out of the file as well. It is the only honest document in it.
lines.plain: Then also remove my architecture note from the tender file. It is the only honest document in that file.

lines.text: The note stays. It goes to every bidder on the same morning, with everything else you have seen since January. And the criteria come from the Charter, not from Amsterdam. Onboard a new instrument in six weeks — SC3, down from nine months. Zero manual re-keying — SC4, down from fourteen hundred fields a quarter. Neither sentence names anybody.
lines.plain: The note stays in the file. Every company that bids receives it on the same morning, with everything else you have seen since January. And the criteria come from the Project Charter, not from the Amsterdam demonstrations. Set up a new lending product in six weeks: that is success criterion SC3, down from nine months. No payment fields typed by hand: that is SC4, down from about 1,400 fields every three months. Neither sentence names a company.

lines.text: Six weeks reads generously beside forty minutes.
lines.plain: Six weeks sounds very generous next to forty minutes.

lines.text: Six weeks is what the Business Case promised the Board. We do not move a target because a sales engineer was quick.
lines.plain: Six weeks is what the Business Case promised the Board. We do not change a target because one sales engineer worked fast.

lines.text: You asked me to check the framework.
lines.plain: You asked me to check the framework contract.

lines.text: It covers everything. Four years of work has gone through it.
lines.plain: It covers everything. We have run four years of work through it.

lines.text: It covers staff augmentation and infrastructure. Nikola's days come through it. A licensed lending platform with implementation and fourteen years of migration does not. There is no mini-competition to run.
lines.plain: It covers extra staff and infrastructure. Nikola's working days are paid through it. It does not cover a licensed lending platform with implementation work and fourteen years of data migration. So we cannot hold a mini-competition under it.
g: framework contract
a contract agreed in advance with suppliers, under which later orders are placed
mini-competition
a short tender held only between the suppliers already on a framework contract
ref: Identify any constraints that may affect the outsourcing process (an organisation's pre-existing agreements or preferred suppliers may require the project team to work with specific suppliers or contractors).

lines.text: That is four months.
lines.plain: That costs us four months.

lines.text: Four months already in the schedule. Open tender under the procurement code, section three point one, two paragraphs. Award the eighteenth of September, Release 1 the twenty-sixth of March 2027, Release 2 the seventeenth of December 2027 — dated in the plan, so the contractor has to hold people against them.
lines.plain: Those four months are already in the schedule. It will be an open tender under the ESM procurement rules. That goes in section 3.1, in two paragraphs. The contract is awarded on 18 Sep 2026, Release 1 on 26 Mar 2027, Release 2 on 17 Dec 2027. The dates are in the plan, so the supplier must keep staff available for them.
g: open tender
a purchase competition open to any company that meets the published conditions
ref: Provide a timeline for all the contracted activities and deliverables. This will ensure that the contractor is committed to having resources available to meet the pre-agreed timeline.

lines.text: Who talks to them?
lines.plain: Who is allowed to speak to the supplier?

lines.text: I do. Sole interface. Their project manager reports to me and escalates to the Steering Committee if he has to. I approve timesheets and purchase orders. Florence accepts deliverables. Your board authorises the award.
lines.plain: I am. I am the only contact point. Their project manager reports to me, and goes to the Steering Committee only if he must. I approve timesheets and purchase orders. Florence Nightingale accepts the deliverables. Your board approves the contract award.
ref: Decide who can interface with the contractors and who is responsible for signing the contract.

lines.text: And what do they hand over besides working software?
lines.plain: And what do they give us besides working software?

lines.text: Configuration manuals, an operations runbook, the migration mapping, the interface specifications. Named as deliverables, so in 2028 they are an obligation and not a favour.
lines.plain: Configuration manuals, an operations handbook, the data migration mapping, and the interface specifications. They are named as deliverables, so in 2028 they are a contractual duty and not a favour.
ref: Identify any documentation deliverables expected from the contractors (e.g. manuals, etc.).

lines.text: Then weight the headings before an envelope opens. Not after.
lines.plain: Then decide how much each criterion counts before any offer is opened. Not afterwards.
ref: The Project Steering Committee (PSC) ensures that the contractor is chosen according to the organisation's processes and standards and to the criteria defined for the project.

choice.prompt: The evaluation criteria have to be written this week. What goes into section four?
choice.promptPlain: The evaluation criteria must be written this week. What do you put in section 4 of the plan?

options.t: Three weighted headings drawn from the Charter's success criteria — technical capability, quality of work, previous euro-area lending or treasury experience — weighted before any offer is opened, with Nikola's exclusion from the panel recorded.
options.tPlain: Three headings taken from the Charter's success criteria: technical capability, quality of work, and previous experience with euro area lending or treasury systems. Decide their weights before any offer is opened, and write down that Nikola cannot sit on the evaluation panel.

reply.text: Fixed in advance, in writing, and no one person able to move them. That is all the sentence in the guide is asking for, and it is the only protection the losing bidders get.
reply.plain: The criteria are fixed in advance, written down, and no single person can change them. That is all the rule in the guide asks for. It is also the only protection the companies that lose will have.

options.why: Step 3 on p.48 wants the criteria listed so that selection rests on pre-set criteria and no single person or group influences the decision. Anchoring them to SC3 and SC4 keeps them traceable to what the Business Case promised, and recording the exclusion of a bidder's own employee is what makes the sentence true rather than decorative.
options.whyPlain: Step 3 on page 48 asks for the criteria to be listed, so that the supplier is chosen on criteria set in advance and no single person or group can influence the decision. Linking the criteria to SC3 and SC4 keeps them connected to what the Business Case promised. Writing down that an employee of a likely bidder cannot judge the offers is what makes the rule real instead of decorative.
ref: List the evaluation criteria for contractors. This ensures that a contractor is selected on the basis of pre-set criteria and that no single person or group influences the decision.

options.t: Write the technical criteria from the Amsterdam demonstration. We have seen it done, so we are entitled to require it.
options.tPlain: Write the technical criteria from what was shown in Amsterdam. We saw it done, so we can require it.

reply.text: And in two years an auditor reads your criteria beside their brochure and finds the same eleven words. I would rather not spend that afternoon.
reply.plain: And in two years an auditor will read your criteria next to their sales brochure and find the same eleven words. I would prefer not to spend that afternoon explaining it.

options.why: Criteria copied from one supplier's demonstration are criteria written by that supplier. The guide's whole reason for step 3 is that no single person or group influences the decision (p.48), and the influence here is external. The Steering Committee later has to be able to say the contractor was chosen by the organisation's processes and the project's criteria (p.85), which it cannot if the criteria were reverse-engineered from a stage act.
options.whyPlain: Criteria copied from one supplier's demonstration are criteria written by that supplier. Step 3 on page 48 exists so that no single person or group can influence the decision, and here the influence comes from outside. Later the Steering Committee must be able to say the supplier was chosen by the organisation's process and the project's criteria (page 85). It cannot say that if the criteria were copied from one stage demonstration.
ref: The Project Steering Committee (PSC) ensures that the contractor is chosen according to the organisation's processes and standards and to the criteria defined for the project.

options.t: Let Nikola draft the technical capabilities section. He knows LOS better than anyone in the building and the criteria will be sharper for it.
options.tPlain: Let Nikola write the section on technical capabilities. He knows LOS better than anyone here, and the criteria will be better.

reply.text: They would be sharper. They would also be mine, and my employer is going to bid, and you would have to explain the difference to somebody who was not in this room.
reply.plain: They would be better criteria. They would also be my criteria, and my employer will bid for this work. You would then have to explain the difference to somebody who was not in this room.

options.why: The plan must identify constraints affecting the outsourcing process, and a seconded architect employed by a probable bidder is exactly such a constraint (p.48). His technical knowledge is still usable — as an input to the requirements, published to every bidder on the same day — but the person who writes the measuring stick cannot be paid by one of the things being measured.
options.whyPlain: The plan must record the constraints that affect the purchase, and an architect employed by a likely bidder is one of them (page 48). His technical knowledge can still be used: it goes into the requirements, and every bidder receives it on the same day. But the person who writes the measure cannot be paid by one of the companies being measured.
ref: Identify any constraints that may affect the outsourcing process (an organisation's pre-existing agreements or preferred suppliers may require the project team to work with specific suppliers or contractors).

options.t: Leave the criteria out. Procurement writes them into the tender documents, and the plan should not duplicate another document.
options.tPlain: Leave the criteria out of the plan. Procurement writes them into the tender documents, and the plan should not repeat another document.

reply.text: Then the first written record of how we choose is written after we have met the people we are choosing between. Procurement will ask you for them anyway, in June, and you will write them in an afternoon.
reply.plain: Then the first written record of how we choose is created after we have already met the companies. Procurement will ask you for the criteria in June anyway, and you will write them in one afternoon.

options.why: Avoiding duplication is a real PM² guideline, but it belongs to the acceptance plan's relationship with the quality and requirements plans (p.49), not here. Listing the evaluation criteria is step 3 of the Outsourcing Plan itself (p.48). The plan is what the tender documents are drawn from, and it is approved by the AGB before the tender exists.
options.whyPlain: Avoiding duplication is a real PM² rule, but it applies to the acceptance plan and its relationship with the quality and requirements plans (page 49). It does not apply here. Listing the evaluation criteria is step 3 of the Outsourcing Plan itself (page 48). The tender documents are written from this plan, and the governance body approves it before any tender exists.
ref: List the evaluation criteria for contractors. This ensures that a contractor is selected on the basis of pre-set criteria and that no single person or group influences the decision.

you.o: Responsible for the Outsourcing Plan. Now drafting section 4, the evaluation criteria, for AGB approval.
you.k: Knows the plan goes to the Corporate Investment Board, and that no framework covers this purchase.
you.w: Wants criteria written from SC3 and SC4 rather than from a supplier demonstration.
you.f: Afraid a criterion shaped by Amsterdam makes the whole tender challengeable in September.

leonardo.o: Solution Provider. Reviews the plan and supports it; not the approver of the criteria.
leonardo.k: Has watched eleven suppliers present and believes he can now recognise a good one.
leonardo.w: Wants the technical bar set high enough that a weak supplier cannot clear it.
leonardo.f: Afraid an open tender costs four months and produces a worse platform than the one he saw.

tesla.o: Lead Solution Architect on the Core Team, seconded from Levallois Systems under the IT framework.
tesla.k: Knows the demonstration was staged, and knows his employer intends to bid for this work.
tesla.w: Wants his architecture note kept in the tender file and his judgement treated as technical, not commercial.
tesla.f: Afraid he is about to be treated as a supplier rather than as an engineer.

gantt.o: Project Support Office. Checked the framework contract's coverage at the Project Manager's request.
gantt.k: Knows the IT framework covers staff and infrastructure, not a licensed platform with migration.
gantt.w: Wants the constraint written into section 3 before anyone assumes a mini-competition.
gantt.f: Afraid the project plans four months of tender it has not scheduled anywhere.

medici.o: AGB chair. Accountable for the Outsourcing Plan he will be asked to approve in June.
medici.k: Knows only what the plan tells him, which is why he asks who signs and who talks.
medici.w: Wants the interface, the signing authority and the documentation deliverables named.

Business implementation may be run inside the project or as a separate one — an organisational choice. RASCI: AGB I, PSC I, PO A, BM R, BIG C, SP I, PM S, PCT I. Approver: the Project Owner alone. The Business Implementation Checklist is set up from this plan, is one of the six PM² checklists, has no RASCI row, and legitimately still carries open lines at closure because business implementation outlives the project. notePlain: Rule: steps 1 to 7 of the Business Implementation Plan on page 52, together with Manage Business Implementation on page 84. The plan must describe the situation before and after the project and the effect on processes, people and culture. It must plan the redesign of the affected business processes. It must set out a communication strategy and the change-management activities. It must name where resistance may come from and study the attitudes of key people. It must decide the training needs. It must put all the project's business implementation activities into the Project Work Plan. And it must name the change work the organisation will carry out after the project ends, possibly as follow-up projects. The organisation may run business implementation inside the project or as a separate project. RASCI: Project Owner Accountable, Business Manager Responsible, Project Manager Supporting, business group Consulted, everyone else Informed. Approver: the Project Owner, alone. The Business Implementation Checklist is built from this plan. It is one of the six PM² checklists, it has no responsibility row, and it correctly still has open items when the project closes, because business change continues after the project. Pages 52 and 84.

note: Guide check: section 6.9, p.53. RfE, Ready for Executing, is the second phase gate. The Project Manager uses the outputs of the Planning Phase to assess whether the goals of the phase have been achieved, and then requests approval from the Project Steering Committee to move on to the Executing Phase. If major deviations from the approved Business Case and/or Project Charter are identified, the PSC must receive an additional approval from the Appropriate Governance Body before the project can move on. PM² supplies a template Phase Exit Review Checklist per phase to guide the assessment alongside a review of the phase's specific goals; the Planning sheet runs to forty-three checks and its compliance percentage is a status indicator, not an authorisation. RASCI: none — the checklist has no row and nobody approves it. Approver of the transition: the Project Steering Committee, which authorises transition between phases unless the Appropriate Governance Body does (p.25). CASTOR baselined the Project Handbook and the Project Work Plan on 26 Jun 2026, cleared the RfE gate on 03 Jul 2026 and holds the Executing Kick-off Meeting on 10 Jul 2026. Pages 25 and 53.
notePlain: Rule: Ready for Executing is the second gate (page 53). The Project Manager uses the results of the Planning Phase to judge whether the goals of that phase were reached, and then asks the Project Steering Committee to approve the move to the Executing Phase. If there are major differences from the approved Business Case or Project Charter, the Steering Committee must also get approval from the Appropriate Governance Body before the project may continue. PM² provides one Phase Exit Review Checklist template per phase, used together with a review of the goals of the phase. The Planning sheet has 43 checks. Its compliance percentage shows status. It does not authorise anything. There is no RASCI row for the checklist and nobody approves it. The move to the next phase is approved by the Project Steering Committee, which authorises transitions between phases unless the governance body does it instead (page 25). In Project CASTOR the Handbook and the Work Plan were baselined on 26 Jun 2026, the gate was passed on 03 Jul 2026, and the Executing Kick-off Meeting is on 10 Jul 2026. Pages 25 and 53.
